rv.q: None of this takes away from the full-bodied intensity of the production, which is fantastically original, gripping and magnificent to the end.
Visually arresting and hugely melodramatic, it is a perfect metaphor for the characters’ long-buried emotions rising up like a dark tide, capsizing the rigidly ordered security of their lives.
This is splashy event theatre, where star casting, the high-wire work of Simon Stone’s process, and the technical sophistication of the Bridge Theatre collide.
Stone’s Lady from the Sea is a tonally uneven play with a weird relationship with the source material and plenty of moments of pure indulgence.
Stone’s dialogue crackles with wit, particularly between Edward, his daughters (Gracie Oddie-James and Isobel Akuwudike) and his old friend Lyle (John Macmillan, very funny and frank).
Nonetheless, Lincoln and Vikander keep us gripped as the implausibilities mount.
Stone’s 2016 adaptation of Federico García Lorca’s Yerma with Billie Piper was an Olivier-winning triumph; here, his brilliance comes only in waves.
It’s Succession -level skilful moment by moment, but alienatingly relentless en masse.
It's an unlikely showcase for the talents of a confident Andrew Lincoln and Oscar winner Alicia Vikander, who seems understandably adrift making her stage debut in this directionless play.
Instead, courtesy of Simon Stone’s revisionist modernising of the play’s setting and references, it has been electrified and positively zings and spits with vitality.
It is a hugely enjoyable evening, full of insight and provocation.

Stone’s overly long Act II could definitely benefit from a dramaturgical cut, with so many competing ideas and characters fighting for centre stage, but his work remains, as ever, ambitious and thought-provoking in how it takes old texts and turns them into something new.

In fact, it slackens just when it needs most to itensify, and I couldn't help but feel as if a running time notably shortened early in the run might have led to the elimination of scenes needed for greater emotional amplitude.
A waste of a powerful story, great cast and my time.

cn.t: Mixed reviews greet Simon Stone's Ibsen reworking, with critics praising Vikander and Lincoln's performances but divided on the overlong, uneven adaptation.

vr.q: It's an intense piece of theater that I wouldn't have wanted to miss, and I give it four stars.
